sources.title: Opet Festival
sources.consultation: Indexed text read 2026-11-14: 11 days from II Akhet 15 under Thutmose III; 24 days (II Akhet 19 – III Akhet 12) in the Medinet Habu calendar, perhaps 27 by the end of Ramesses III’s reign; barks of Mut, Khonsu and the king by Tutankhamun.

sources.title: Festival dates
sources.consultation: Indexed text read 2026-11-14 (the page itself returned an error): Valley Festival at the new moon of the tenth month; Opet start dates under Thutmose III and Ramesses III.

sources.title: The Khoiak festival
sources.consultation: Read 2026-11-14: fourth month of the flood season; seeded earth figures of Osiris; rites at Karnak on days 18–26 with a procession of Osiris on day 26 (Papyrus Louvre N 3176); Osiris chambers found at Karnak.

sources.title: Dates and precursors of the Opet Festival
sources.consultation: Indexed text read 2026-11-14: civil year of three seasons of four 30-day months plus five extra days, drifting against the solar year; Thutmose III’s Opet dates.

sources.title: Sex and booze figured in Egyptian rites

sources.title: Heb-Sed
sources.consultation: Read 2026-11-14: celebrated by the king after 30 years of rule and repeated every 3 years thereafter.

sources.title: Some new evidence for the processional way of the Beautiful Feast of the Valley at Western Thebes
sources.consultation: Indexed text read 2026-11-14: the Decade festival, when Amun of Luxor crossed to Djeme (Medinet Habu) to visit the buried primeval gods; earliest mention under Thutmose II.

sources.title: Herodotus, Histories 2.37 (trans. A. D. Godley, 1920)
sources.consultation: Read 2026-11-14: priests shave the whole body every other day, wear one linen garment and papyrus sandals, wash in cold water twice a day and twice a night; no fish; beans unclean. A Greek visitor’s account of the 5th century BC.

sources.title: Temple Personnel (World Eras: Ancient Egypt)
sources.consultation: Read 2026-11-14, Purity section: three baths a day in the sacred lake in the Ramesside period; natron mouth-rinse; hair removal; circumcision; abstinence before and during service; no wool; regional food taboos. Draws on Sauneron, Quirke, Shafer and Wilkinson.

sources.title: Turin Indictment Papyrus (P. Turin Cat. 1887), translation and record
authors: ELEPHANTINE project, Staatliche Museen zu Berlin
sources.publisher: Staatliche Museen zu Berlin – Elephantine database
sources.consultation: Read 2026-11-14: verso lines 9–11, a priest entered “under the god” after 7 days of drinking natron, with 3 days still due. Reigns of Ramesses IV–V.

sources.title: A. M. Blackman, article in Recueil de travaux relatifs à la philologie et à l’archéologie égyptiennes et assyriennes (1921), p. 46
sources.consultation: Text of p. 46 seen in a search extract 2026-11-14 (the page itself is bot-protected): priests’ purification before their course included “drinking” natron; the king-priest was robed and anointed after purification; the House of the Morning. Old study; flagged for checking against a modern source.

sources.title: God’s Wife of Amun
sources.consultation: Search extract read 2026-11-14: highest-ranking priestess of the Amun cult; Ahmose-Nefertari’s appointment recorded on a stela at Karnak; scenes of her purified in the sacred lake and following the king into the sanctuary. Overview; flagged for replacement by Ayad 2009.

sources.title: Relief Fragment of Shepenwepet II (74.99.2)
sources.consultation: Label read 2026-11-14: relief from a chapel in North Karnak; a God’s Wife of Amun, a celibate high priestess, wearing a vulture headdress; about 700 BC.

sources.consultation: Read 2026-11-14 (search extract): the God’s Wife shown making herself pure to enter the temple and taking precedence over male priests; chapels built mostly at Karnak in Dynasties 23–26.
